extracted.intended_audience: college mathematics instructors and mathematics education researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for designing and implementing assessment in problem-centered undergraduate (and graduate) college mathematics courses, including formative techniques, group and individual assessment, journals, projects, and exam design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment during problem solving
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment should occur as students are engaged in problem solving/learning mathematics rather than as a separate activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect assessment data while students work on nonroutine problems (classwork, homework, group work) so that competence and reasoning processes are visible; avoid treating assessment as an isolated event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on students' problem-solving explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment and classroom environment should emphasize students’ explanations of their methods rather than prescribed procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negotiate a classroom environment that values students' explanations and reflections; ask questions like 'how did you think to do this?' and favor understanding of reasoning over rote procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of generalizable and elegant solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizable and elegant solutions are explicitly valued as indicators of mathematical competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While valuing elegance, allow any method students choose; note distinctions between elegant/generalizable approaches and nongeneralizable methods (trial-and-error, exhaustive search). Use examples in feedback to point out elegance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written feedback comments (no points) on homework
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide written feedback in the form of comments on homework rather than assigning points or grades for every homework item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comments such as 'very nice,' 'I do not follow,' or 'how did you get this?' to prompt reflection. Reserve numerical grades for other components and let comments guide learning; avoid early penalties for weak work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homework as primary assessment data source
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular reading of homework is the richest source of assessment data because it reveals students’ competence and reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track homework over time to chart progress; identify weaknesses (e.g., geometry, proportional reasoning) and use this to design targeted tasks or reteaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class presentations for validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Students present solutions to the class for validation; there is no single method expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use presentations to expose students to multiple solution approaches; encourage voluntary contributions and note changes in engagement (e.g., students initiating board work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing group dynamics and individual involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: During small-group work, assess who initiated ideas, who listened, and each student’s involvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructor should make notes on group interactions, monitor participation, and use observations as part of the assessment record; shuffle groups during the term to broaden interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic final grading based on end-of-course competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Final course grades should reflect students’ progression and level of competence at the end of the course rather than an average of recorded numerical scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider all available information (homework, classwork, exams, presentations) and give particular attention to final competence; early weaknesses should not unduly penalize final grades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exam design: take-home and in-class, comprehensive finals
rubrics_metrics.description: Midterms and finals should mirror nonroutine problems used in class; examinations may include both take-home and in-class portions, with the comprehensive final consisting of ~10 challenging problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Announce that an A on the final indicates course-level excellence (might determine an A in the course); design exams to assess deep problem solving rather than only procedural skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage student self-assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Students are encouraged to assess their own work and submit the grade they believe they should receive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use self-evaluations as a basis for discussion; instructor retains final grade authority but uses student reflection to inform grading conversations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of daily/weekly journals for formative feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Daily journal writing provides one-on-one written dialogue between student and teacher, promoting reflection and formative evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample template: (1) In class, I felt..., (2) In class, I learned..., (3) The most positive result..., (4) The least positive result..., (5) Additional comments. Score journals by giving a point per entry and read weekly (3–5 minutes per student). Answer every journal entry, try to be positive, and use entries to guide instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group work as instantaneous assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: In-class group work offers immediate assessment opportunities and supports peer learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques: form groups of 3–4, circulate to give feedback, use 'Pass the Chalk' to ensure all members contribute (no spectators). Observe and record who contributes; use class groupwork to prepare students for homework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Team tests and group grading practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Teams may complete joint tests; if all contribute equally, all team members receive the same grade for the group test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow 7–10 days for team tests; require each contributing member to sign each problem they helped solve; teams may consult texts and each other but not external groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative projects to increase engagement and understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign creative projects (models, concept maps, poems, designs, numeration systems) to help students visualize and integrate concepts and to connect mathematics to real life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: physical inverse-function models, pipe-cleaner/inverse constructions, concept maps for conic sections, designing a numeration system for a planet. Use projects as a stimulus for research, reflection, and to build enthusiasm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start small and iterate; preserve lectures
rubrics_metrics.description: When implementing new assessment methods, begin on a small scale, be willing to fail and try again, but do not abandon lectures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lectures provide needed background; combine brief lectures with active/problem-centered practice. Shuffle group members and maintain instructor responsiveness to journal concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender-sensitive practices to support female students
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment techniques that work well for female students include journal writing, group work, daily assessment, hands-on approaches, creative projects, and emphasizing collaboration over competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize creativity, real-life connections, problem posing, debates and discussions; provide formative evaluation and practices that build self-efficacy and confidence (e.g., models, collaborative tasks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adult-learner accommodations and scaffolding
rubrics_metrics.description: For adult learners, use short mini-lectures (10–15 minutes), sequenced questions to spark discussion, opportunities for presentations, and flexible policies to reduce test anxiety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include offering to drop the first exam if below 70, lengthening mini-lectures to 20–25 minutes if needed, providing closure at end of class, and offering extra demonstrations of technology (TI-92/DERIVE).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperative learning structure for adult classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Cooperative learning with groups of 4–5, a group leader, and individual accountability helps adult learners develop pacing and self-assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require individual copies of solved problems in each student’s handwriting; warn against 'sponges' who do not contribute; give group grades for projects but individual grades for classwork/participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examinations requiring 'show all work' and anxiety-reducing options
rubrics_metrics.description: Design exams (14–20 questions) that require students to show all work so instructors can see thinking; provide options to reduce anxiety (e.g., dropping a low first exam).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use show-work requirement to diagnose needs; offer drop policies and other flexibility to relieve test anxiety particularly for older students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of technology and lab projects to motivate learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate technology projects (graphing calculators, computer algebra systems like DERIVE, web research) to motivate and teach skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide tutor and lab support; assign projects that require researching mathematical connections (e.g., Mathematics and Nature) and producing designs that use scaling, symmetry, parametric/polar equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use assessment findings to adjust instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use careful reading of homework, journals, and other assessment data to choose and design tasks that target observed weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If many students struggle with a topic, reteach or slow pace; if few do, offer targeted study sessions; use assessment evidence to redesign learning activities and assignments.
